passage:
The PG in Koramangala had old cupboards, so on his first weekend Lalit bought a second padlock, a small door alarm, and a steel box for his laptop charger and passport. He tested the alarm four times. Santosh, his roommate from Nashik, watched from the top bunk.
"Chalo, dosa," Santosh said, lifting his helmet off the hook. Lalit climbed on pillion without one. "It's only two signals away."
On the flyover a bus cut across and Santosh braked hard. Lalit grabbed the seat, heart thudding. At the dosa place he laughed it off, then opened the alarm app to make sure nothing in the room had moved.
Santosh looked at him over the chutney. "Your cupboard is safer than your head, yaar."

qa.q: What did Lalit buy on his first weekend at the PG?
qa.a: Lalit bought a second padlock, a small door alarm, and a steel box for his laptop charger and passport.

qa.q: Why do you think Lalit checked the alarm app right after the near miss?
qa.a: Locking the cupboard down completely gave him a feeling of total control, so that small fear kept pulling at him while the bigger road danger got laughed off.

qa.q: What small change would protect Lalit most?
qa.a: Getting a helmet of his own and wearing it on every ride, even for two signals; one padlock is plenty for the cupboard.

qa.q: How does Santosh see Lalit's priorities?
qa.a: Santosh finds them upside down, joking that the cupboard is safer than Lalit's head, and was probably shaken too after braking hard.

grounding: It shows a student fixating on removing a small theft fear while ignoring the far bigger danger of riding without a helmet.

passage:
"So? Did you apply for the research assistant post?" Chandrika asked, stirring the rasam.
"No, Amma. I took the library desk job."
"The library? Sachin, Professor Nair himself told you to apply. The lab pays three times more, and it's your own subject."
"Twenty people are applying. What if I don't get it? The library is sure. They said yes the same day."
"And if you do get it?"
"If, Amma. With the library there's no if."
Chandrika put the ladle down. "You'll stamp books all summer when you could be learning from him."
"At least I won't sit at home waiting for an email." He glanced at his phone. "The deadline's tonight anyway."
"Tonight means it's still open," she said, and pushed the laptop toward him.

qa.q: Which job did Sachin take?
qa.a: Sachin took the library desk job.

qa.q: What is Sachin afraid of when he says "With the library there's no if"?
qa.a: He is afraid of applying and being turned down; the sure yes feels comforting even though the lab post pays more and fits his subject.

qa.q: What could Sachin try before the deadline tonight?
qa.a: He could still send the application and keep the library job as a fallback, so he gets a chance at the better option without giving up the sure one.

qa.q: How does Chandrika see Sachin's choice?
qa.a: She sees him settling for stamping books when he could be learning in the lab, and she pushes gently because the chance is still open tonight.

grounding: It shows a student taking a low but certain option over a much better uncertain one, because certainty feels safe.

passage:
I'm Mahima. Last month Sharmila and I took the night bus back to Indore after a college fest. I was obsessed with my phone. I'd heard about phones being stolen on buses, so I zipped it into a pouch, put the pouch in my bag, and slept with the bag strap round my wrist. I woke up every hour to check.
The bus dropped us at the highway stop at one in the morning. The road to our hostel was dark and empty. Sharmila said, "Let's wait for an auto at the dhaba, it's lit." I said no, it's only ten minutes, let's walk.
We made it fine. But I've thought about it since: I guarded a phone all night and then walked two girls down a dark road without a second thought.

qa.q: Where did the bus drop Mahima and Sharmila?
qa.a: The bus dropped them at the highway stop at one in the morning.

qa.q: Why did Mahima wake up every hour on the bus?
qa.a: Mahima was fixated on the phone being stolen and wanted that one risk brought down to nothing, so checking felt necessary.

qa.q: What would a wiser plan for that night have looked like?
qa.a: Keep the phone reasonably safe and actually sleep, then wait for an auto at the lit dhaba as Sharmila suggested, since the dark road was the bigger danger.

qa.q: What might Sharmila have felt walking down the dark road?
qa.a: Sharmila may have felt uneasy and unheard 😟, having suggested waiting somewhere lit and then been overruled.

grounding: It shows a student fixating on eliminating a small fear of theft while ignoring the larger danger of a dark, empty road.

passage:
Warden's note, Boys' Hostel B, Tuesday. Parveen.
Imran (second year) came to the office for the third time this month asking for a stronger lock for his cupboard. He has already fitted two. He keeps no cash at all, in case of pickpockets, and asked whether we could put a camera outside his room. I understand the worry; there was one theft on his floor last year.
But this morning I watched him ride out of the gate on his motorbike without a helmet, as he does every day, overtaking a bus on the main road. When I mentioned it, he laughed. "It's a five-minute ride, ma'am."
What I did next: I didn't lecture. I sat with him and asked him to list what he was most afraid of losing, and which of those a cupboard could protect. He went quiet. I've kept a spare helmet at the gate, and I'll check in with him next week.

qa.q: How many locks has Imran already fitted on his cupboard?
qa.a: He has already fitted two.

qa.q: Why might the cupboard lock feel more urgent to Imran than a helmet?
qa.a: There was a real theft on his floor, so that fear feels close and fixable, while the helmetless ride has become routine and he tells himself it's only five minutes.

qa.q: What was the turning point in the warden's approach, and why might it work?
qa.a: Instead of lecturing, Parveen asked Imran to list what he feared losing and what a cupboard could protect, so he could see the bigger danger for himself.

qa.q: How might Parveen feel watching Imran overtake a bus without a helmet?
qa.a: She is likely alarmed and protective, because the risk she sees on the road is far bigger than the one he keeps asking her to fix.

grounding: A warden notes a student who fixates on removing a small theft risk while ignoring the much bigger danger of riding without a helmet.

passage:
Thursday, hostel room, 11 p.m.
Took the data-entry job at the college office today. Four hours every afternoon, fixed small pay, no interview, no chance of rejection.
Swati thinks I've lost it. The coaching centre near the gate wants chemistry tutors and pays almost three times more for fewer hours, and Ma'am Rao from our department practically told me I'd get it. But there's a demo class, and a panel, and what if they say no? Then I'd have nothing. This way I have something for sure.
Swati said, "Neelam, you'd rather have a sure little than a likely lot." I told her she doesn't understand.
Typing spreadsheets at four today, I kept thinking about the chemistry notes I love making for juniors. It's fine. It's safe. It's fine.

qa.q: What job did Neelam take at the college office?
qa.a: The data-entry job, four hours every afternoon.

qa.q: What does Neelam repeating "It's fine. It's safe. It's fine" suggest?
qa.a: It suggests Neelam is trying to quiet a doubt, feeling the comfort of a certain job while sensing the better chance given up 😔

qa.q: What choice could Neelam still make without losing the sure job?
qa.a: Neelam could still ask for the demo class; a no would leave the data-entry job in place, so the fear of ending up with nothing isn't real.

qa.q: Why might Swati see the choice so differently from Neelam?
qa.a: Swati looks at the pay, the hours and Ma'am Rao's confidence, while Neelam mostly feels the fear of rejection, so to Swati it looks like giving up a lot for a little.

grounding: A student takes a low but certain job over a much better one because avoiding any chance of rejection feels safer.
